title: ACC/Everlaw GenAI Survey 2025: In-House Legal's AI Adoption Surge
author: Association of Corporate Counsel · Everlaw

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The survey accepts the cluster’s supervised workflow-reconfiguration framing and materially extends it with buyer-side evidence: in-house teams expect GenAI to shift drafting, contract management, research and some higher-level work internally, while responsible use retains human oversight. Its findings are mainly adoption data and respondent expectations, not proof of autonomous legal capability or realised displacement.
qs: Backed by current and anticipated efficiency gains, most respondents see an opportunity to reshape their operations by insourcing drafting (78%), contract management (71%), and research (62%), along with elements of higher-level work such as M&A (29%) and litigation (29%).

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The survey accepts the cluster’s human-led, work-redesign framing and materially extends it with buyer-side evidence that in-house departments expect GenAI to reshape insourcing, service delivery, costs and pricing. It also reinforces the gap between adoption and realised organisational value, while treating human oversight as necessary. Its evidence is primarily respondent practice and expectations, not direct testing of jagged task capability or productivity.
qs: “In-house counsel are not only using AI to make their departments more efficient — they are reimagining how legal work is delivered, how costs are being managed, and how value is defined.

“Generative AI — used responsibly and always with a human in the loop — will allow law firms to deliver services faster, smarter, and within clients’ ever-tighter budgets.”  “The speed of adoption of artificial intelligence within the workplace speaks volumes,” said Veta T.

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: The survey directly supports the proposition that corporate legal departments are becoming the principal channel for AI gains: adoption is increasing, departments expect greater self-sufficiency and insourcing, and buyers plan to press outside counsel on delivery and pricing. It also reinforces the synthesis’s caution that these are primarily expectations and intentions, because most respondents have not yet seen tangible law-firm savings.
qs: -  **Reliance on outside counsel is shrinking: **As in-house legal teams are using GenAI for efficiency and to increase self-sufficiency, nearly two-thirds (64%) expect to rely less on outside counsel, an increase from 58% in 2024, and 50% expect reduced outside counsel costs, up from 46%.

-  **Clients will challenge the billable hour: **While 59% report no GenAI savings from their law firms yet, only about a quarter (24%) are satisfied with how outside counsel are adopting GenAI tools for cost effectiveness.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The survey supports the cluster’s account of accelerating GenAI adoption and a prospective shift in work and bargaining power toward in-house legal departments. Respondents report opportunities to reshape operations through insourcing and expect less reliance on outside counsel, although these are perceptions and forecasts rather than demonstrated market-wide transfers or realised cost reductions.

kp.d: The third annual ACC/Everlaw report, released on October 14, 2025, surveys 657 in-house legal professionals across 30 countries. The source explicitly limits year-over-year comparisons to U.S. respondents; its findings combine reported adoption and experiences with expectations about future impacts.
qs: The report, based on a survey of 657 in-house legal professionals across 30 countries, provides a comprehensive look at the current state of GenAI adoption within corporate legal departments.
Year-over-year comparisons are for U.S. respondents only.

kp.k: GenAI adoption doubles as organizational prohibitions decline
kp.d: Among U.S. respondents, active GenAI use rose from 23% in 2024 to 52% in 2025. Passive planning halved to 14%, while company-policy prohibitions fell from 29% to 9%. The release also reports that only 2% have no plans to use GenAI.
qs: Active use of GenAI technology has jumped to 52% this year, more than double the 23% reported in 2024.
This year’s survey shows adoption of GenAI for legal work more than doubled to 52 percent among U.S. respondents over last year, while those just passively planning for use halved to 14 percent.
Only 9% now say company policy prohibits GenAI use, down sharply from 29% last year.
Only 2% have no plans to use GenAI.

kp.k: Respondents increasingly anticipate significant or transformative impacts
kp.d: Half of respondents characterize AI's anticipated impact as significant, and 20% call it transformative, compared with 11% last year. Expectations of moderate impact fell from 37% to 25%. These are respondents' assessments of impact, not demonstrated organizational transformation; year-over-year comparisons concern U.S. respondents.
qs: Half (50%) say AI’s impact will be significant, and one in five (20%) now call it transformative, nearly double last year’s 11% figure.
Those expecting only a “moderate” impact fell from 37% to 25%.

kp.d: The survey reports that 91% cite efficiency gains, versus 86% last year, while 49% see better client service, versus 38%, and 34% see stronger decision-making, versus 16%. These are survey-reported benefits rather than separately measured performance results; the source limits annual comparisons to U.S. respondents.
qs: 91% of legal professionals cite efficiency gains, up slightly from 86% last year.
Far more now see better client service (49%, up from 38%) and stronger decision-making (34%, up from 16%).

kp.k: In-house teams anticipate reduced outside counsel dependence
kp.d: Nearly two-thirds (64%) expect to rely less on outside counsel, compared with 58% in 2024, and 50% expect lower outside counsel costs, compared with 46%. The release connects these expectations to greater efficiency and self-sufficiency. Despite its heading asserting shrinking reliance, the numerical evidence concerns expectations, not realized reductions.
qs: As in-house legal teams are using GenAI for efficiency and to increase self-sufficiency, nearly two-thirds (64%) expect to rely less on outside counsel, an increase from 58% in 2024, and 50% expect reduced outside counsel costs, up from 46%.

kp.k: Insourcing opportunities encompass routine and strategic legal work
kp.d: Respondents identify opportunities to insource drafting (78%), contract management (71%) and research (62%), alongside elements of M&A (29%) and litigation (29%). The source distinguishes existing use for core-task efficiencies from opportunities to internalize more strategic work, with control over data-intensive processes and costs as stated motivations.
qs: Legal teams are already using GenAI to realize efficiencies in core tasks like drafting and contract management.

Backed by current and anticipated efficiency gains, most respondents see an opportunity to reshape their operations by insourcing drafting (78%), contract management (71%), and research (62%), along with elements of higher-level work such as M&A (29%) and litigation (29%).

Professionals now see an opportunity to handle more strategic work — such as litigation and M&A — internally rather than outsourcing it to regain control over data-intensive processes and control costs.

kp.k: Outside counsel adoption lacks transparency and realized savings
kp.d: The source reports that a majority of in-house professionals lack visibility into law firms' GenAI use. Separately, 59% report no GenAI savings from their firms yet, and only 24% are satisfied with outside counsel's adoption for cost effectiveness. It recommends communicating how adoption produces efficiencies and client savings to strengthen relationships.
qs: A majority of in-house professionals lack visibility into how their law firms are using GenAI and report no tangible cost savings so far.
While 59% report no GenAI savings from their law firms yet, only about a quarter (24%) are satisfied with how outside counsel are adopting GenAI tools for cost effectiveness.
By effectively communicating how GenAI adoption translates into efficiencies and savings for clients, outside counsel can build relationships based on shared value and stand out from the competition.

kp.k: Client pressure could change delivery and billing models
kp.d: A majority (61%) plan to press their GenAI-using law firms for changes in service delivery and pricing, while 49% predict client demand will drive billing changes. The source does not claim the billable hour has ended; it predicts a competitive advantage for firms translating AI efficiencies into transparent, value-based billing.
qs: A new survey conducted by Everlaw and the Association of Corporate Counsel (ACC) found that a majority (61%) of survey respondents said they plan to push for change in how legal services are delivered and priced from their law firms that use GenAI.
A majority (61%) plan to push for change in how legal services are delivered and priced, and half (49%) predict client demand will be the primary driver of billing changes.
The billable hour’s reign is far from over, but its future is on a collision course with client expectations.
Law firms that are proactive about how GenAI-powered efficiencies translate into transparent, value-based billing will gain the competitive edge.

kp.k: European respondents lead reported adoption and optimism
kp.d: The release identifies Europe as having the highest adoption and optimism globally: 61% report using GenAI in legal practice and 29% expect transformative effects for legal teams. It also says European respondents are more likely to report outside counsel cost savings, without providing a percentage for that comparison.
qs: With 61% of respondents already using GenAI in legal practice and 29% expecting its impact to be transformative for legal teams, Europe shows the highest rates of adoption and optimism globally.
European respondents are also more likely to see cost savings from outside counsel.

kp.k: Everlaw's efficiency prediction requires human involvement
kp.d: Everlaw Chief Legal Officer Gloria Lee predicts faster, smarter and more budget-compatible law-firm services, explicitly conditioning that prediction on responsible GenAI use with a human in the loop. This is an attributed executive view, not a survey finding or a claim supporting autonomous substitution.
qs: “Generative AI — used responsibly and always with a human in the loop — will allow law firms to deliver services faster, smarter, and within clients’ ever-tighter budgets.”

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: ACC and Everlaw report accelerating GenAI adoption, falling policy barriers, and growing expectations of substantial effects on corporate legal departments.
pts.d: The source reports active use rising from 23% in 2024 to 52% in 2025, with year-over-year comparisons restricted to U.S. respondents. Company-policy prohibitions fell from 29% to 9%. Half describe AI's expected impact as significant and 20% as transformative, compared with 11% previously; these are respondents' assessments rather than measured transformation. European respondents report 61% adoption and 29% expecting transformative impact, described by the source as the highest adoption and optimism globally.

pts.k: ACC and Everlaw report perceived benefits extending beyond efficiency to client service and decision-making.
pts.d: The survey summary says 91% cite efficiency gains, 49% see better client service, and 34% see stronger decision-making, versus 86%, 38%, and 16% respectively in the previous year. ACC president and CEO Veta T. Richardson characterizes in-house adoption as a rethinking of delivery, costs, and value, not merely departmental efficiency.

pts.k: Respondents expect GenAI to enable insourcing and reduce reliance on outside counsel and associated costs.
pts.d: ACC and Everlaw report that 64% expect less reliance on outside counsel, up from 58%, and 50% expect lower outside counsel costs, up from 46%. Respondents identify insourcing opportunities in drafting (78%), contract management (71%), research (62%), and elements of M&A and litigation (29% each). Although a heading describes reliance as already shrinking, the supporting figures concern expectations and opportunities rather than measured reductions in outsourcing or spending.

pts.k: ACC and Everlaw predict buyer pressure on legal-service delivery and billing, while reporting limited realized savings from outside counsel.
pts.d: The source reports that 59% have not yet received GenAI savings from their law firms and only 24% are satisfied with outside counsel's adoption for cost effectiveness. It reports 61% planning to push for delivery and pricing changes, and 49% predicting client demand will primarily drive billing change. The landing page predicts competitive advantages for firms that transparently connect AI efficiencies to value-based billing; it does not claim the billable hour has already disappeared.

pts.k: The source presents transparent communication and human-supervised AI use as routes to improved outside-counsel value.
pts.d: The ACC/Everlaw landing page says most in-house professionals lack visibility into law firms' GenAI use and argues that communicating efficiencies and savings can strengthen client relationships and differentiation. Separately, Everlaw Chief Legal Officer Gloria Lee predicts faster, smarter services within tighter budgets, expressly conditional on responsible use with a human in the loop. Her claim concerns augmentation, not unsupervised replacement of lawyers.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is an annual survey of 657 in-house legal professionals across 30 countries; strategic forecasts also draw on organizational commentary.
pts.d: The October 14, 2025 press release summarizes the third annual ACC/Everlaw survey. Adoption, benefits, barriers, satisfaction, intentions, and expectations are presented as respondent reports. The supplied text does not provide sampling procedures, response rates, subgroup sizes, objective productivity measurements, or audited spending outcomes. Predictions of competitive advantage and improved service are source commentary or attributed executive statements, not separately demonstrated outcomes. The unrelated case-study links are not evidence for the survey's market predictions.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Reported conditions concern 2025, with U.S.-only comparisons to 2024; outsourcing and pricing forecasts have no specified completion date.
pts.d: The source was released October 14, 2025. Its year-over-year comparisons must not be interpreted as global trends because the survey explicitly restricts those comparisons to U.S. respondents. Insourcing and lower outside-counsel costs are anticipated developments supported by current and expected efficiencies. Pricing pressure is an intention, while the absence of savings is reported as the current position. Lee's service-improvement prediction requires responsible human-supervised use, and the claimed competitive advantage requires transparent translation of efficiencies into billing value.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Corporate legal departments are the adopting buyers; outside law firms face prospective changes in demand, transparency expectations, and pricing.
pts.d: In-house legal professionals and general counsel are portrayed as gaining capacity, improving service and decisions, and potentially bringing more work inside their organizations. Corporate clients may gain greater control over data-intensive work and lower external costs. Outside law firms face possible reduced reliance on their services, pressure to demonstrate savings, and opportunities to differentiate through transparent value-based billing. Europe is highlighted as a regional adoption leader. The source does not make specific predictions about associate staffing, ALSP market share, or access to justice for underserved individuals.
